candidates.workingClaim: February 15, 1965: On February 15, 1965, Canada officially adopted the Maple Leaf Flag following a royal proclamation.
February 15, 1898: On February 15, 1898, an explosion sank the US battleship Maine while it lay at anchor in Havana Harbor, Cuba.
February 15, 1989: On February 15, 1989, the Soviet Union withdrew its last troops from Afghanistan, which it had occupied since 1979.
February 15, 1820: On February 15, 1820, Susan B. Anthony, a pioneer of the women's suffrage movement, was born in Adams, Massachusetts.
February 15, 1564: On February 15, 1564, Galileo Galilei was born in Pisa. He later discovered the four largest moons of Jupiter, now called the Galilean moons.

February 16, 2005: On February 16, 2005, the Kyoto Protocol, an agreement to reduce emissions of gases that contribute to global warming, went into effect, eight years after its adoption in Kyoto, Japan.
February 16, 1918: On February 16, 1918, the 20-member Taryba, Lithuania's national council, proclaimed the country an independent state.
February 16, 1937: On February 16, 1937, the DuPont chemist Wallace Hume Carothers patented nylon.
February 16, 1959: On February 16, 1959, Fidel Castro became premier of Cuba.
February 16, 1861: On February 16, 1861, President-elect Abraham Lincoln stopped at Westfield, New York, and met 12-year-old Grace Bedell, who had written to suggest that he grow a beard.
February 17, 1996: On February 17, 1996, world chess champion Garry Kasparov triumphed over IBM's Deep Blue computer.
February 17, 2008: On February 17, 2008, Kosovo declared its independence from Serbia, though a number of countries refused to recognize the new republic.
February 17, 1864: On February 17, 1864, the Confederate submarine Hunley became the first submarine to sink an enemy ship when it attacked the USS Housatonic off Charleston, South Carolina.
February 17, 1904: On February 17, 1904, Giacomo Puccini's Madama Butterfly premiered at La Scala in Milan. It became one of the most frequently performed operas.
February 17, 1801: On February 17, 1801, following a tie in the electoral college, the US House of Representatives elected Thomas Jefferson president.
February 18, 1930: On February 18, 1930, Clyde Tombaugh, a 24-year-old American with no formal training in astronomy, discovered the dwarf planet Pluto.
February 18, 1546: On February 18, 1546, Martin Luther, leader of the Protestant Reformation, died at age 62 in Eisleben, Saxony.

February 18, 2006: On February 18, 2006, the American speed skater Shani Davis won the men's 1,000-meter long-track final, becoming the first Black athlete to win an individual Winter Olympics gold medal.
February 18, 1933: On February 18, 1933, the artist and musician Yoko Ono was born.
February 18, 1836: On February 18, 1836, the Hindu mystic and priest Ramakrishna was born in Hooghly (now Hugli), Bengal, India.
February 19, 1473: On February 19, 1473, the astronomer Nicolaus Copernicus was born in Torun, Poland. He argued that Earth is a planet that orbits the Sun.
February 19, 1878: On February 19, 1878, the American inventor Thomas Edison patented the phonograph, a device that reproduced sound through a needle's vibration.
February 19, 1942: On February 19, 1942, US President Franklin D. Roosevelt signed Executive Order 9066, which forced Japanese Americans into detention camps during World War II.
February 19, 1997: On February 19, 1997, the Chinese leader Deng Xiaoping died at age 92.
February 19, 2008: On February 19, 2008, Fidel Castro, after 19 months out of the public eye, formally resigned as president of Cuba.
February 20, 1962: On February 20, 1962, John H. Glenn, Jr., became the first American to orbit Earth, circling it three times.
February 20, 1943: On February 20, 1943, the volcano Paricutin, in Michoacan state, Mexico, began erupting.
February 20, 1909: On February 20, 1909, the Italian writer Filippo Tommaso Marinetti coined the term Futurism in the Paris newspaper Le Figaro.
February 20, 1902: On February 20, 1902, the American photographer Ansel Adams was born.
February 20, 1844: On February 20, 1844, the Austrian physicist Ludwig Boltzmann was born.
February 21, 1972: On February 21, 1972, Richard Nixon became the first sitting US president to visit China.
February 21, 1916: On February 21, 1916, the Battle of Verdun, one of the most devastating engagements of World War I, began.
February 21, 1965: On February 21, 1965, Malcolm X was assassinated while giving a speech in Manhattan.
February 21, 1925: On February 21, 1925, the American weekly magazine The New Yorker began publication under its editor Harold W. Ross.

February 21, 1952: On February 21, 1952, students and activists protested at the University of Dhaka for recognition of their language, Bangla (Bengali). Police opened fire, killing seven people. UNESCO later chose February 21 as International Mother Language Day.
